div.head: EGu 2
div.ab: ⁊ gif hwá Cristendom wyrde oððe hæþendom weorþige wordes oððe weorces, gylde swa wer swa wite swa lahslitte, be þam þe syo dæde sy.
⁊ gyf hwá Cristendom wyrde oððon hæðendom weorðige wordes oððe weorces, gylde swa wer swa wite swa lahslite, be ðam ðe seo dæd sy.
Et si quis christianitatem (suam) malemittat uel paganismum ueneretur uerbis uel operibus, reddat sic weram sic wytam sic lahslite, secundum quod factum est.
⁊ gif hwá Cristendom wyrde oððe hæþendom weorþige wordes oððe weorces, gylde swa wer swa wite swa lahslitte, be þam þe syo dæd sy.
And gif hwa Cristendom wyrde oððe hæþendom weorþige wordes oððe weorces, gylde swa wer swa wite swa lahslitte, be þam þe syo dæd sy.

Und wenn jemand Christenthum verletzt oder Heidenthum ehrt mit Wort oder Werk, zahle er entweder [sein] Wergeld oder Strafgeld, beziehungsweise [in Dena lage] Rechtsbruchbusse, [je] nachdem wie die That sei.

And if anyone violates Christianity or honours heathenism in word or deed, let him pay either [his] wergeld or a fine, or [in the Danelaw] the penalty for breach of law, according to what the deed is.
If anyone offends against the Christian religion, or honours heathen practices by word or deed, he shall pay either wergeld or fine or lahslit, according to the nature of the offence.
And if anyone violates Christian practice or shows reverence for heathenism by word or deed, he must pay either his wergild or a penalty or lahslit, according to the nature of the deed.
div.note: lahslit: Having no adequate modern English equivalent, lahslit is a term of Old Norse derivation used by Wulfstan to denote the Danish analogue to English “wergild” (literally, “man-price”: an amount of money determined by rank paid by the responsible party as compensation for the injury or death of another). A partial sense of the values attached to lahslit can be gleaned from the prescriptions in The Northumbrian Priests’ Law 51–54.

Später wird Christentum zu beobachten zwar oftmals befohlen, aber es zu verletzen nicht mehr mit Strafgeld bedroht
Later the observance of Christianity is indeed often commanded, but its violation is no longer threatened with a fine
Vgl. Gl Christentum 2a
Cf. Gl Christentum 2a

Vgl. Pro, 1³. ‘Wort und Werk’, häufige Phrase (s. Wb: word 2), meint wohl heidnisch-mythologischen Redegebrauch neben Götzendienst oder abergläubischer Handlung gemäss Nordischer Religion. S. Gl Wergeld 30c

Cf. Pro, 1³. ‘Word and deed’, a frequent phrase (see Wb: word 2), probably means heathen-mythological usage of speech alongside idolatry or superstitious practice according to Norse religion. See Gl Wergeld 30c
‘Je nach Schwere des Falles’ am Satzschlusse gehört logisch hierher
‘According to the gravity of the case’ at the end of the sentence belongs here logically
‘30 Schil., wo Englisches Recht in Ostanglien herrscht’ (laut 3, 1) = 150 Pfg.; nur diesen entspricht Dän. Rechtsbruchbusse; s. d. Gl 3. 4
‘30 shill. where English law prevails in East Anglia’ (according to 3, 1) = 150 pence; only to this does the Danish compensation for breach of law correspond; see that word in Gl 3. 4

Die Ergänzung folgt aus 3, 1ff. Die hier gemeinten 12 Ör = 3 Halbmark zahlen später nur Gemeinfreie, Adlige mehr; Northu 50f. = In Cn I 612. Die seit höchstens 1—2 Menschenaltern bekehrten Nordleute zahlen also für Religionsverbrechen mehr als die alten Christen. Doch liegt dies wohl nicht am Fanatismus der Missionare, sondern am Beibehalten alter Strafgeldfixa

The supplement follows from 3, 1ff. The 12 ores meant here = 3 half-marks are later paid only by common freemen, nobles paying more; Northu 50f. = In Cn I 612. The Northmen, converted at most 1–2 generations before, thus pay more for religious offences than the old Christians. This is probably due, however, not to the fanaticism of the missionaries but to the retention of old fixed amounts of fines
Das Gericht entscheidet über die Schwere der Strafe; s. d. Gl 13
The court decides on the severity of the punishment; see that word in Gl 13
Das unorganische -e (s. d. Wb 2) in H bezeichnet späte Sprache
The inorganic -e (see that word in Wb 2) in H indicates late language
Scand. Lit. ‘a breach of the law,’ then the fine incurred thereby.
